Meanwhile, [Sergio Ramos](/wiki/Sergio_Ramos "Sergio Ramos") has accumulated the most caps while playing for the club, with 176.

**Salem** ([/ˈseɪ.ləm/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:LL-Q1860_(eng)-Flame,_not_lame-Salem.wav "File:LL-Q1860 (eng)-Flame, not lame-Salem.wav"), [*SAY-ləm*](/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")) is the [capital city](/wiki/List_of_capitals_in_the_United_States "List of capitals in the United States") of the [U.S. state](/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [Oregon](/wiki/Oregon "Oregon"), and the [county seat](/wiki/County_seat "County seat") of [Marion County](/wiki/Marion_County,_Oregon "Marion County, Oregon"). It is located in the center of the [Willamette Valley](/wiki/Willamette_Valley "Willamette Valley") alongside the [Willamette River](/wiki/Willamette_River "Willamette River"), which runs north through the city. The river forms the boundary between Marion and [Polk](/wiki/Polk_County,_Oregon "Polk County, Oregon") counties, and the city neighborhood of [West Salem](/wiki/West_Salem,_Salem,_Oregon "West Salem, Salem, Oregon") is in Polk County.

The population was 175,535 at the [2020 census](/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"),[[5]](#cite_note-2020_Census_(City)-5) and was estimated to be 180,406 in 2024,[[6]](#cite_note-USCensusEst2024-6) making it the [second-most populous city](/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Oregon "List of cities in Oregon") in the state after [Portland](/wiki/Portland,_Oregon "Portland, Oregon") and before [Eugene](/wiki/Eugene,_Oregon "Eugene, Oregon").

Salem is the principal city of the [Salem metropolitan area](/wiki/Salem_metropolitan_area_(Oregon) "Salem metropolitan area (Oregon)") that covers Marion and Polk counties and had a combined population of 433,353 at the [2020 census](/wiki/2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census") and was estimated to have a population of 443,416 in 2024. fanoutqa_039550.t: List of countries by coffee production :: chunk_0000
fanoutqa_039550.x:
List of countries by coffee production :: chunk_0000
This is a **list of countries by coffee production**, based on data from the [Food and Agriculture Organization](/wiki/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization "Food and Agriculture Organization") (FAO) for 2023. This data covers the production of [green coffee beans](/wiki/Green_coffee_bean "Green coffee bean"), the primary ingredient in the production of processed coffee. Roasting and packaging of [ground coffee](/wiki/Ground_coffee "Ground coffee") often takes place after it has been exported from the producing nation; see the separate [list of countries by coffee exports](/wiki/List_of_countries_by_coffee_exports "List of countries by coffee exports").

Coffee is a [cash crop](/wiki/Cash_crop "Cash crop") in many areas, with the amount produced for export significantly in excess of local demand. Several of these countries maintain substantial [supply-chain relations](/wiki/Supply_chain_management "Supply chain management") with the [world's largest coffeehouse chains](/wiki/List_of_coffeehouse_chains "List of coffeehouse chains") and enterprises.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Often these coffeehouse chains pay a [premium](/wiki/Premium_pricing "Premium pricing") above market price in order to alleviate [fair trade](/wiki/Fair_trade "Fair trade") and [sustainable farming](/wiki/Sustainable_agriculture "Sustainable agriculture") concerns. Developing countries that participate in the coffee market wield considerable influence on [global coffee economics](/wiki/Economics_of_coffee "Economics of coffee").[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)

World War II :: Course of the war :: War breaks out in Europe (1939–1940) :: part 02 :: chunk_0016
After the outbreak of war in Poland, Stalin threatened [Estonia](/wiki/Estonia "Estonia"), [Latvia](/wiki/Latvia "Latvia"), and [Lithuania](/wiki/Lithuania "Lithuania") with military invasion, forcing the three [Baltic countries](/wiki/Baltic_states "Baltic states") to sign [pacts](/wiki/Background_of_the_occupation_of_the_Baltic_states#Soviet_ultimatums_and_occupation "Background of the occupation of the Baltic states") allowing the creation of Soviet military bases in these countries; in October 1939, significant Soviet military contingents were moved there.[[83]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmithPabriksPursLane200224-86)[[84]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBilinsky19999-87)[[85]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurrayMillett200155–56-88) [Finland](/wiki/Finland "Finland") refused to sign a similar pact and rejected ceding part of its territory to the Soviet Union. [The Soviet Union invaded Finland](/wiki/Winter_War#Soviet_invasion "Winter War") in November 1939,[[86]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESpring1986207–226-89) and was subsequently expelled from the [League of Nations](/wiki/League_of_Nations "League of Nations") for this crime of aggression.[[87]](#cite_note-90) Despite overwhelming numerical superiority, Soviet military success during the [Winter War](/wiki/Winter_War "Winter War") was modest, and the Finno–Soviet war ended in March 1940 with [some Finnish concessions of territory](/wiki/Moscow_Peace_Treaty "Moscow Peace Treaty").[[88]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHanhimäki199712-91)

In June 1940, the Soviet Union [occupied](/wiki/Soviet_occupation_of_the_Baltic_states_(1940) "Soviet occupation of the Baltic states (1940)") the entire territories of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania,[[84]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBilinsky19999-87) as well as the Romanian regions of [Bessarabia, Northern Bukovina, and the Hertsa region](/wiki/Soviet_occupation_of_Bessarabia_and_Northern_Bukovina "Soviet occupation of Bessarabia and N

Brown joined [YouTube](/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") in 2011 while at university after he saw Josh gaining traction on the platform and then decided to become a full-time [YouTuber](/wiki/YouTuber "YouTuber") after university.[[2]](#cite_note-SidemenBook-2)[[1]](#cite_note-YTStats-1) He uploads [video game commentaries](/wiki/Let%27s_Play "Let's Play"), most notably of the *[FIFA](/wiki/FIFA_(video_game_series) "FIFA (video game series)")* and *[NBA 2K](/wiki/NBA_2K "NBA 2K")* video game series, as well as [football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football") challenges, [vlogs](/wiki/Vlog "Vlog"), and comedy-style videos.[[5]](#cite_note-SundayTimes2019-6)[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-9)

On 19 October 2013, Brown and four other British YouTubers formed the entertainment collective Ultimate Sidemen, later shortened to simply [Sidemen](/wiki/Sidemen "Sidemen"). Since 2014, the group has consisted of seven British YouTubers: [Vikram Barn](/wiki/Vikkstar123 "Vikkstar123") (Vikkstar123), [Josh Bradley](/wiki/Zerkaa "Zerkaa") (Zerkaa), [Harry Lewis](/wiki/Wroetoshaw "Wroetoshaw") (W2S), [Simon Minter](/wiki/Miniminter "Miniminter") (Miniminter), [JJ Olatunji](/wiki/KSI "KSI") (KSI), [Ethan Payne](/wiki/Behzinga "Behzinga") (Behzinga), and Tobi Brown (TBJZL).[[9]](#cite_note-10) The group produces online videos, consisting of challenges, sketches, and video-game commentary, as well as selling exclusive Sidemen merchandise.[[10]](#cite_note-11)[[11]](#cite_note-12)

In September 2019, Brown was listed as the 38th most influential online creator in the United Kingdom by *[The Sunday Times](/wiki/The_Sunday_Times "The Sunday Times")*.[[5]](#cite_note-SundayTimes2019-6)

fanoutqa_005758.x:
Essential amino acid :: Interchangeability :: chunk_0011
The distinction between essential and non-essential amino acids is somewhat unclear, as some amino acids can be produced from others. The [sulfur](/wiki/Sulfur "Sulfur")-containing amino acids, [methionine](/wiki/Methionine "Methionine") and [homocysteine](/wiki/Homocysteine "Homocysteine"), can be converted into each other but neither can be synthesized *de novo* in humans. Likewise, cysteine can be made from homocysteine but cannot be synthesized on its own. So, for convenience, sulfur-containing amino acids are sometimes considered a single pool of nutritionally equivalent amino acids as are the [aromatic](/wiki/Aromatic "Aromatic") amino acid pair, [phenylalanine](/wiki/Phenylalanine "Phenylalanine") and [tyrosine](/wiki/Tyrosine "Tyrosine"). Likewise [arginine](/wiki/Arginine "Arginine"), [ornithine](/wiki/Ornithine "Ornithine"), and [citrulline](/wiki/Citrulline "Citrulline"), which are interconvertible by the [urea cycle](/wiki/Urea_cycle "Urea cycle"), are considered a single group.

Meanwhile, Napoleon never gave up hope of detaching him from the coalition. Busan :: Names :: chunk_0006
The name "Busan" is the [Revised Romanization](/wiki/Revised_Romanization_of_Korean "Revised Romanization of Korean") of the city's name. The name 부산 has been recorded since the late 15th century.[[13]](#cite_note-14) "Busan" officially replaced the earlier [McCune–Reischauer](/wiki/McCune%E2%80%93Reischauer "McCune–Reischauer") romanization *Pusan* in 2000.[[14]](#cite_note-15)[[b]](#cite_note-19) During the [Japanese colonial period](/wiki/Korea_under_Japanese_rule "Korea under Japanese rule"), the Japanese reading of the city's name was "Fuzan" which may have remained in the maps that Americans used during the Korean war.

The name 釜山 (now written 부산 using the [Korean alphabet](/wiki/Hangul "Hangul")) is [Sino-Korean](/wiki/Sino-Korean_vocabulary "Sino-Korean vocabulary") for "Cauldron Mountain", believed to be a former name of Mt Hwangnyeong ([Korean](/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language"): 황령산; [Hanja](/wiki/Hanja "Hanja"): 荒嶺山; [RR](/wiki/Revised_Romanization_of_Korean "Revised Romanization of Korean"): *Hwangnyeongsan*) west of the city center. The area's ancient state Mt Geochil (거칠산국; 居柒山國; *Geochilsan-guk*, "Rough-Mountain Land") is similarly thought to refer to the same mountain, which towers over the town's harbor on the Suyeong (the later Silla district of Geochilsan-gun was renamed [Dongnae](/wiki/Dongnae "Dongnae") in 757).[[18]](#cite_note-20)

Main article: [2017 Rafael Nadal tennis season](/wiki/2017_Rafael_Nadal_tennis_season "2017 Rafael Nadal tennis season")

At the [Brisbane International](/wiki/2017_Brisbane_International "2017 Brisbane International") Nadal lost to [Milos Raonic](/wiki/Milos_Raonic "Milos Raonic") in the quarterfinals.[[289]](#cite_note-291) Nadal began the Australian Open with straight-set wins over [Florian Mayer](/wiki/Florian_Mayer "Florian Mayer") and [Marcos Baghdatis](/wiki/Marcos_Baghdatis "Marcos Baghdatis"), before more difficult wins over [Alexander Zverev](/wiki/Alexander_Zverev_Jr. "Alexander Zverev Jr.") and [Gaël Monfils](/wiki/Ga%C3%ABl_Monfils "Gaël Monfils"), to reach his first Grand Slam quarterfinal since the [2015 French Open](/wiki/2015_French_Open "2015 French Open"). Nadal beat Raonic and [Grigor Dimitrov](/wiki/Grigor_Dimitrov "Grigor Dimitrov"), to set up a final against Federer, his first Grand Slam final since he won the 2014 French Open. Nadal lost to Federer in five sets; the first time that Nadal had lost to Federer in a Grand Slam since the [2007 Wimbledon Championships](/wiki/2007_Wimbledon_Championships "2007 Wimbledon Championships").

At [Acapulco](/wiki/2017_Abierto_Mexicano_Telcel "2017 Abierto Mexicano Telcel") lost to [Sam Querrey](/wiki/Sam_Querrey "Sam Querrey") in the final. Nadal lost to Federer in the fourth round at [Indian Wells](/wiki/2017_BNP_Paribas_Open_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_singles "2017 BNP Paribas Open – Men's singles") and the [Miami](/wiki/2017_Miami_Open_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_singles "2017 Miami Open – Men's singles") final.[[290]](#cite_note-292) Nadal then won his 29th Masters title in Monte Carlo; his tenth title, the most wins by any player at a single tournament in the Open Era.[[291]](#cite_note-293)
